new_entities.title: Ẹgbẹ́ Awo
new_entities.description: The ancient, sacred guild and consecrated fraternal institution governing all initiated practitioners of the Ifá epistemological and divinatory canon across Yorùbáland and the diaspora.
new_entities.etymology_and_philosophy: Linguistically compounded from 'ẹgbẹ́' (confraternity, guild, or societal assembly) and 'awo' (esoteric mystery, metaphysical secret, or sacred wisdom), Ẹgbẹ́ Awo denotes the sacred collective custody of cosmological knowledge. Historically governed under the supreme primacy of the Àràbà Àgbàyé of Ilé-Ifẹ̀ alongside imperial and regional Arabas across every historic Yorùbá kingdom, Ẹgbẹ́ Awo functions as the judicial, educational, and ethical bedrock of ancestral guidance. The philosophy of the guild dictates that wisdom belongs to Olódùmarè and is channeled through Orúnmìlà, mandating that every initiated priest maintain rigorous truthfulness (Òtítọ́), noble character (Ìwà-Pẹ̀lẹ́), and selfless communal service without exploiting the vulnerable.
new_entities.historical_timeline: Dating back to the classical antiquity of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, Ẹgbẹ́ Awo emerged as the primary epistemological council advising monarchs, war generals, and communal elders. Throughout the classical epochs of Old Ọ̀yọ́, Òwu, Ìjẹ̀bú, and Kétu, royal Babalawos formed permanent advisory bodies that ratified coronation rites and military campaigns. Through centuries of transatlantic upheaval and down into the contemporary era, Ẹgbẹ́ Awo maintains standardized curricula, peer review, and ancestral ordination lineages spanning West Africa, Cuba, Brazil, and worldwide Ifá academies.
new_entities.material_and_craftsmanship: Regalia and apparatus associated with Ẹgbẹ́ Awo include the sacred Apo Ifá (divination bag of handwoven asọ-òkè or beaded leather), the Ọ̀pá Ọ̀rẹ̀rẹ̀ (iron herbalist-diviner staff surmounted by birds), the consecrated Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ chain, Ikin sacred palm nuts, and the carved Opon Ifá tray dusted with Ìyẹ̀ròsùn powder.
new_entities.social_and_ritual_context: The guild convenes regularly during lunar Itadogun (16-day) assemblies, annual Ifá festivals, and state crises. It oversees the rigorous ethical examinations, herbal apprenticeships, and ordination rituals (Ìtẹ́fá) of novitiates, ensuring that neither charlatans nor unverified doctrines pollute the sacred lineage.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Awo níí gbé awo ní’kọ̀kọ̀; b’awo kò bá gbé awo ní’kọ̀kọ̀, awo á tẹ́ (An initiate elevates and shields a fellow initiate in secret; when initiates fail to uphold each other, the mystery loses its sacred honor).
Bí a bá tẹ́ awo tán, awo a tún ara rẹ̀ tẹ́ (After an initiate undergoes ordination, they must continually re-discipline and purify their own character).
A kì í fi awo dán wò; awo kì í ṣe ohun àṣedánwò (One does not toy with sacred mysteries; sacred wisdom is not a subject of reckless experimentation).
new_entities.diaspora_connections: Preserved seamlessly within Cuban Lucumí and Regla de Ocha as the Consejo de Mayores and Babalawo fraternities, and in Brazilian Candomblé Ketu and modern international Ifá federations.

new_entities.title: Ẹgbẹ́ Olórìṣà
new_entities.description: The organized body, priesthood orders, and consecrated devotees dedicated to the communal veneration, shrine preservation, and liturgical propitiation of the Òrìṣà pantheon.
new_entities.etymology_and_philosophy: Formed from 'ẹgbẹ́' (guild/collective) and 'olórìṣà' (possessor or custodian of an Orisha, from 'ní' + 'òrìṣà'), Ẹgbẹ́ Olórìṣà embodies the human covenant with celestial divinities. Philosophically, the guild bridges human reality with transcendent spiritual archetypes, asserting that divinities thrive on human devotion, ethical harmony, and sacred offerings (ẹbọ), while humans derive protection, fertility, and balance from divine Àṣẹ.
new_entities.historical_timeline: Originating in the primordial ancestral shrines of Yorùbáland, Ẹgbẹ́ Olórìṣà organized dedicated lineages around specific divinities—such as the Ẹlẹ́gbẹ́ Ṣàngó in Ọ̀yọ́, the Ẹlẹ́gùn Ọ̀ṣun in Òṣogbo, and the Agbede-Ogun guild across all metallurgical towns. These orders survived colonial religious displacement and flourished across the African Diaspora in Cuba, Brazil, Trinidad, and North America.
new_entities.material_and_craftsmanship: Members carry specialized sacred emblems: Ìlèkè (consecrated glass beads tailored to each deity's color symbolism), Ọ̀ta (sacred river stones housing the divinity's spirit), Ìke (carved ivory armlets), and cast bronze, brass, or iron implements forged by sacred metalsmiths.
new_entities.social_and_ritual_context: Acts as the cultural lifeblood of town festivals, sacred dances, trance possession liturgies, healing ceremonies, and regular shrine offerings. The elders of Ẹgbẹ́ Olórìṣà ensure proper ritual protocols are observed during annual civic festivities.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Orìṣà b’ó o lè gbè mí, fi mí sílẹ̀ bó o ti bá mi (Divinity, if you cannot uplift me, leave me in the state you originally met me).
Ẹni tó bọ Òrìṣà t’ó tẹ̀lé ìlànà kò ní d’arúgbó lásán (Whoever venerates the divinities and observes moral principles shall never grow old in despair).
Òrìṣà ti a bọ̀ tí kò gbè wá, a kì í sọ pé kò sí mọ́; àwọn kan ń jẹ àǹfààní rẹ̀ (A divinity that hasn't answered our plea is not dead; others are actively receiving its blessings).
new_entities.diaspora_connections: Directly institutionalized as the Ilé Orisha, Casas de Santo, and Terreiros of Candomblé Ketu and Santería / Regla de Ocha across the Americas.

new_entities.title: Àwọn Ìyá Àgbà Ìjọ́yè
new_entities.description: The august college of supreme matriarchal priestesses, royal female dignitaries, and shrine custodians who exercise supreme ancestral authority, spiritual oversight, and dynastic balance in traditional Yorùbá governance.
new_entities.etymology_and_philosophy: Composed of 'àwọn' (plural marker), 'ìyá' (mother), 'àgbà' (elder/venerable), and 'ìjọ́yè' (titled dignitary), this concept reflects the foundational Yorùbá metaphysical principle of maternal sovereignty: 'Ìyá ni wúrà' (Mother is pure gold) and the primordial authority of the feminine matrix. In royal palaces, particularly in the imperial court of Old Ọ̀yọ́ and Ilé-Ifẹ̀, these high priestesses stood above even the monarch in esoteric rank, presiding over coronation oaths, royal ancestral vaults (Bàrá), and imperial shrine sanctums.
new_entities.historical_timeline: Established during the earliest classical foundation of the Ọ̀yọ́ and Ifẹ̀ monarchies, titles such as Iyamode, Iyaláṣẹ, and Iyá Nṣo held profound constitutional power. In the Ọ̀yọ́ court, the Aláàfin kneeled only before the Iyamode as the living representative of the deified royal ancestors. They maintained perpetual custody of the dynastic regalia, mediated between the crown and the cosmological energies of Ìyámi, and preserved the spiritual immunity of the kingdom.
new_entities.material_and_craftsmanship: Their regalia comprises consecrated handwoven Kìjìpá and Aṣọ-Òkè robes in deep ancestral indigo, heavy heirloom coral and jasper beads (Ìyùn), intricately beaded leather staffs, and the sacred calabashes of divine authority (Igbá Àṣẹ).
new_entities.social_and_ritual_context: They perform the secret accession rites of kings, maintain the sacred fires of ancestral shrines, mediate high dynastic disputes, and ensure balance between masculine executive power and primordial maternal mystical energy.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọba ń bọ̀ lẹ́yìn Ìyá; Ìyá l’ó bí Ọba (The King walks behind the Mother; for it is the Mother who births the King).
Àgbàrá kì í ya k’ó sọ p’óun kò mọ odò; ẹnìkan kì í l’ọ́lá k’ó gbàgbé Ìyá (The raging torrent cannot claim it forgets the riverbed; no one achieves supreme renown while ignoring the venerable Mother).
Àṣẹ obìnrin kì í gbẹ́; b’óbìnrin bá fi ọwọ́ rẹ̀ fún un, ó di dandan (The sacred sanction of the matriarch never fails; when a consecrated woman confirms a blessing, it becomes unbreakable law).
new_entities.diaspora_connections: Revered as the founding mothers, Iyalorishas, and Mãe de Santos who established and led the paramount historical Candomblé and Santería temples across Salvador da Bahia, Havana, and Matanzas.

new_entities.title: Ààbò àti Ìbílẹ̀
new_entities.description: The metaphysical, apotropaic, and traditional protective sciences, guardian sentinels, and consecrated barrier rituals dedicated to defending individuals, households, and sovereign communities from unseen malevolent forces.
new_entities.etymology_and_philosophy: Derived from 'ààbò' (protection, defense, sanctuary) and 'ìbílẹ̀' (indigenous, rooted in ancestral soil), this cosmological category encompasses the profound Yorùbá science of spiritual security. Philosophically, traditional defense rests on preserving spiritual equilibrium: fortifying the individual Orí against psychic predation, stationing consecrated sentinels at physical thresholds, and deploying spoken incantations (Ofo) to deflect harm back to its origin.
new_entities.historical_timeline: Developed across millennia of ancestral history and heavily mobilized during pre-colonial inter-kingdom conflicts and the nineteenth-century Kiriji wars, where hunter guilds (Ọdẹ) and warriors (Balógun) relied on consecrated mud guardians, protective amulets, and boundary covenants to safeguard besieged settlements.
new_entities.material_and_craftsmanship: Physical manifestations include consecrated earth and clay sculptures (Sigidi) sculpted with sacred river mud and medicinal herbs, forged iron spikes and padlocks consecrated to Ògún, leather-bound talismans (Ondè), and protective boundary stones buried at threshold crossroads.
new_entities.social_and_ritual_context: Enacted by specialized priests, native doctors (Oníṣègùn), and hunters to protect newborns, safeguard farms from theft, protect compounds against nocturnal witchcraft, and cleanse travelers embarking on hazardous journeys.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ààbò kì í ṣe fún ẹni t’ó gbójú lé ogun; ààbò wà fún ẹni t’ó mọ orí rẹ̀ ní’kọ̀kọ̀ (Protection is not merely for the warrior boasting of battle; protection belongs to the one who reveres their inner destiny in secret).
Ẹni tí Olódùmarè kọ́lé fún, afẹ́fẹ́ kì í gbá a lọ (The house constructed under divine protection cannot be swept away by any tempest).
Ààbò t’ó dára ju ogun lọ; àìbẹ̀rù kọ́ l’ó ń ṣẹ́gun (Prudent spiritual defense is superior to aggressive war; victory comes not from recklessness, but from divine fortification).
new_entities.diaspora_connections: Preserved in Lucumí resguardos and Brazilian patuás and assentamentos de proteção designed to guard spiritual houses from negative intrusion.
